analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a single government health plan covering everyone, with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: Backed by 115 House Democrats but referred to seven committees without a single hearing, markup, or floor vote, the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services covering every U.S. resident. It would cover hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health treatment, dental, vision, reproductive care, gender-affirming care, and long-term care, and would ban deductibles, copays, and surprise charges for covered services. Private insurers and employers could only sell extra coverage on top of the government plan, and Medicare exchanges and other federal programs would wind down. It would phase in over two years, starting with children, seniors, and current Medicare recipients.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or copays for covered care, including the roughly 26 million uninsured and millions more who are underinsured. People who currently skip dental, vision, mental health, or long-term care because of cost would get those covered. People would keep their doctors regardless of insurance networks, and the bill protects workers dislocated from health insurance jobs with retraining funds. Anyone with employer coverage would no longer be tied to a job for insurance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: The bill entitles every U.S. resident to comprehensive coverage including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use treatment, dental, vision, reproductive care including abortion and contraception, gender-affirming care, and long-term care [S2][S3].
It prohibits all cost-sharing — deductibles, coinsurance, copayments — and balance billing for covered services, and eliminates prior-authorization and step-therapy hurdles [S3].
It phases in over two years, with people under 19 and over 55 (plus current Medicare enrollees) covered after one year, and other people able to buy in during the transition [S2].
It requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices and sets up a national health budget with payments to hospitals through negotiated global budgets [S2][S3].

It sets aside at least 1 percent of the health budget for up to five years for wage replacement, retirement benefits, and job training for workers displaced from health insurance administration jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose their core business, since selling coverage duplicative of the government plan would be unlawful. The cost of care now paid through private premiums, employer contributions, and out-of-pocket charges would shift to federal financing — taxes. Brand-name drug makers would face negotiated prices. Employers would no longer be the gatekeepers of health benefits. Hospitals would move to fixed global budgets with a cap on executive compensation, which could mean tighter revenue than today.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, drug makers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not spell out dedicated new taxes to fund the program; it creates a Universal Medicare Trust Fund but the introduced text leaves the financing to be worked out, and economists estimate a national single-payer program would require several trillion dollars a year in federal spending [S3].

The transition would eliminate a large share of health-insurance administration, claims-processing, and billing jobs; the bill acknowledges this and funds retraining with 1 percent of the budget for five years [S3].

Hospitals would be paid through lump-sum global budgets rather than per-patient payments, with capped executive compensation, and HHS would set national coverage determinations for experimental care — critics of single-payer systems warn this can lead to underinvestment in facilities and slower access to new technology [S3].

With no cost-sharing at all, demand for care would likely rise, raising the risk of wait times unless the supply of doctors, nurses, and facilities expands — the bill addresses this with special-projects funding for underserved areas and nurse staffing ratio standards, but does not add clinician supply on its own [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the gain is large and direct: coverage for everything from dental care to long-term care with no out-of-pocket charges, and no more medical bills or insurer denials. The honest counterweight is that the financing burden would have to be created by Congress (this text leaves it blank), the shakeout would cost hundreds of thousands of health-sector administrative jobs, and hospitals would have to learn to run on fixed budgets. Whether total national spending rose or fell depends on design choices that this introduced bill did not yet make. The trade is real and contestable — but the bill never got far enough for any of it to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The Speaker referred it to seven House committees the day it was introduced, one of those committees sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and no committee ever held a markup or the House ever voted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Medicare for All Act on May 17, 2023 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to seven committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Rules, Oversight, Armed Services, and Judiciary [S5].
On May 19, 2023 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and again on December 17, 2024 [S5].
114 members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].
No committee held a markup, no hearing is listed in the action history, and the House never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry and its shareholders kept the existing system intact, since nothing changed. Employers keep their current role in providing coverage, and drug makers avoid the bill's price-negotiation requirement. Nothing changed for patients either — the uninsured and underinsured gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, drug makers, and employers

for.name: Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare for All Act and organized 114 Democratic cosponsors for it.

for.name: 114 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — about a quarter of the House and roughly half of the Democratic caucus — giving it the largest cosponsor list it had received, but none of them were in a position to bring it to the floor.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce; Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the two primary health-care committees in the 118th Congress (Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-WA; Jason Smith, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in either committee during the two-year Congress, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran sustained public and lobbying campaigns against single-payer legislation, which would eliminate their core business of selling primary coverage.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against single-payer proposals that would replace negotiated federal pricing with a system where the government sets drug payment rates for the entire market.

sides.party_line_note: All 115 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; committee chairs in both chambers were Republicans who never scheduled action on it.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for private insurers to sell coverage duplicating the government plan and shuts down the ACA exchanges, eliminating most of the industry's revenue. Insurers earn from premiums, deductibles, and restricting care — costs the bill abolishes.
HHS would be required to negotiate prescription drug prices for the entire market, replacing the current system where Americans pay some of the world's highest drug prices.

Employers would be barred from providing duplicative health benefits, ending their role as gatekeepers of American health coverage; most would shed a major benefit cost, but they would lose a key tool for recruiting and tying workers to jobs.

Hospitals would be paid through fixed global budgets instead of per-service billing — eliminating unpaid care and billing overhead but capping revenue, capping executive compensation, and restricting conflicts of interest between administrators and suppliers.

industries.industry: Health insurance administration and medical billing
industries.note: A large share of claims-processing and billing jobs would disappear under a single payer; the bill would fund wage replacement and retraining with 1 percent of the health budget for five years.

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage middlemen and care coordinators
industries.note: Entities that do not directly provide care — including Medicare Advantage plan intermediaries — would be disqualified from participating in the program.
